title: Presence and typing indicators
description: Project: Presence and typing indicators. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Presence and typing indicators are among the most visible real-time features in a communication platform. They require low latency, efficient broadcasting, and careful throttling to avoid overwhelming the server and distracting users. Senior engineers treat these ephemeral signals as a system design challenge, not just a UI detail.

items: Presence signals online, offline, away, and busy states with low latency and eventual consistency
Typing indicators are transient events that should expire automatically if not refreshed
Throttle typing events on the client to reduce message bus load and network overhead
Broadcast presence changes only to users who care: room members, conversation participants, or team members
Use presence leases: a heartbeat that expires after a timeout, avoiding stale presence when a client crashes
Design the data model for presence to support queries like who is online in this room
Handle the long tail of slow clients that miss heartbeats and need graceful degradation

terms.definition: A time-bounded claim that a user is online, refreshed periodically by a heartbeat and automatically expired if not renewed.
Limiting the rate at which events are sent, typically to the minimum rate that preserves UX.
Delaying an event until the user stops performing an action, used for typing indicators to avoid signaling every keystroke.
Data that is intentionally short-lived and can be safely discarded without persistence.
Sending a message to all subscribers in a channel, which can create a hot-spot if the channel has many members.

data.text: Poorly implemented presence and typing indicators can degrade the entire system. Unthrottled typing events from two hundred users in a channel can generate more messages per second than the chat itself. Stale presence that never expires makes users trust the system less. Getting these features right requires designing for scale from the start.

data.title: Use the smallest useful interval
data.text: A typing indicator should be sent at most once every two to three seconds and expire after five seconds of inactivity. A presence heartbeat every thirty seconds with a ninety-second lease is usually sufficient. Smaller values look better but multiply the load on the message bus.

items: User presence record: userId, status enum, lastSeen timestamp, currentRoomId optional
Room presence set: a Redis sorted set keyed by room ID with scores of lastSeen timestamps
Lease renewal: update lastSeen on each heartbeat; remove entries older than the lease timeout
Status transitions: online to away after thirty seconds of no heartbeat; away to offline after ninety seconds

data.title: Implement presence with Redis sorted sets
data.description: Build a presence system using a Redis sorted set where the score is a Unix timestamp and the member is the user ID. Implement heartbeat renewal, expiry cleanup, and a room membership query.
steps: Create a Redis sorted set per room with key pattern presence:room:{roomId}
On heartbeat, add or update the user ID with the current timestamp as the score
Set a key expiration on the sorted set to ninety seconds to handle abandoned rooms
Query online users with ZRANGEBYSCORE using the current timestamp minus the lease timeout
Implement a cleanup job that removes stale entries every ten seconds
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to query who is currently online in any room with a single Redis command and no stale entries.

items.question: How do I handle timezone differences in presence timestamps?
items.answer: Use UTC timestamps everywhere. Store and compare timestamps as Unix epoch integers. Do not rely on client-local clocks for expiry logic.

items.question: What if a user has multiple tabs open?
items.answer: Track connection count per user. Only broadcast offline when the last connection closes. Use a reference count in Redis: increment on connect, decrement on close, and remove only when the count reaches zero.

items.question: Should I persist presence to PostgreSQL?
items.answer: Persist only if you need historical presence analytics. For real-time queries, Redis is sufficient and far faster. Write to PostgreSQL asynchronously if you need audit logs.

data.title: Summary
points: Presence is ephemeral state; treat it as such in your data model
Throttle typing events to reduce message bus load
Use Redis sorted sets for efficient room-based presence queries
Handle multi-tab presence by tracking connection counts per user
data.takeaway: Presence and typing indicators look simple on the surface, but they require careful rate limiting, expiry, and broadcast design to work at scale.
